prompt.context: Our North Dakota-based client, CDC Pharmaceuticals, manufactures and distributes over-the-counter cold, allergy and flu medicines sold in convenience stores across the United States. CDC's current manufacturing plant is severely outdated, and the company's management team is in the process of evaluating two options for future production.
prompt.question: CDC would like our help in determining whether it should build a new plant or outsource production to a third-party manufacturer.

clarifying_info.q: Where would the new plant be built, and would production be interrupted during construction?
clarifying_info.a: The new plant would be built in North Dakota, and operations would continue throughout the project — no lost production.

clarifying_info.q: Would the choice of manufacturing method affect selling price?
clarifying_info.a: No impact on price; CDC would achieve the same selling price regardless of how or where the products are manufactured.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any capacity constraints under either option?
clarifying_info.a: Capacity is a non-issue for both options.

clarifying_info.q: What is CDC's current production volume?
clarifying_info.a: CDC currently manufactures 50 million units per year.

exhibits.title: Suggested Framework: Financial and Non-Financial Decision Criteria
exhibits.shows: A two-branch framework tree comparing the two options across Financial (Revenues, Costs) and Non-Financial (Operations, Product, Industry/Competition, Image/Strategy) dimensions, with sub-bullets under each branch
exhibits.data: Financial branch — Revenues: Price (impact of manufacturing method on price, quality, consumer preference), Volume (breakeven, capacity, current production vs. demand); Costs: Variable (manufacturing, distribution), Fixed (annual fee to third-party, savings due to outsourcing), Set-up (contract for third-party, investment in plant). Non-Financial branch — Operations: CDC manufacturing capabilities/expertise, production volume flexibility, quality control, ability to diversify/add products; Industry/Competition: industry trend toward/away from outsourcing, competitor use of third-party manufacturers, competitive response; Image/Strategy: community ties gained/lost by building, benefits to producing locally, impact on employee satisfaction (relocations, lay-offs, improved conditions).

framework: Financial analysis — Revenues: assess impact of manufacturing method on selling price and on volume/demand

Financial analysis — Costs: compare variable manufacturing and distribution costs under each option; compare fixed costs (annual third-party fee vs. plant overhead); compare set-up costs (third-party contract vs. new plant capital investment)
Financial analysis — Breakeven: calculate unit volume at which contribution margins equalise; compare to current/projected volume
Non-Financial — Operations: evaluate CDC's in-house manufacturing expertise, flexibility to adjust production volume, quality control, and ability to expand product range
Non-Financial — Industry/Competition: assess whether the industry is trending toward outsourcing; review competitor sourcing strategies and likely competitive responses
Non-Financial — Image/Strategy: consider community and employment impact in North Dakota, local production benefits, and effect on employee satisfaction

questions.prompt: Question 1: How would you evaluate the two options under consideration, and what are some of the factors you would explore in order to help CDC make its decision?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognise this as a framework question. Average responses cover only the financial pros and cons (profit tree). Good responses add non-financial criteria. Great responses build a comprehensive, structured evaluation covering both financial dimensions (revenues, variable/fixed/set-up costs, breakeven) and non-financial dimensions (operations capabilities, industry trends, image and strategy).

questions.prompt: Question 2: At what unit volume are the two options equally attractive for CDC?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute contribution margins for each option, then set up an equation equating total contribution under both options and solve for unit volume. Strong candidates will note that 40 million units is below CDC's current 50 million unit volume, making the new plant immediately more attractive, and will also calculate the new plant breakeven (21 million units, recovered in less than one year), reinforcing the recommendation to build.

math.setup: New Plant: selling price $3.00, manufacturing cost $0.50, set-up cost $52.5 million → contribution margin = $2.50/unit. Third-Party: selling price $3.00, manufacturing cost $0.75/unit for first 20 million units and $0.25/unit for all additional units → contribution margins = $2.25/unit (≤20M units) and $2.75/unit (>20M units). Set up equation equating total contribution: New Plant contribution = Third-Party blended contribution.
steps: Contribution margins: New Plant = $3.00 − $0.50 = $2.50/unit; Third-Party ≤20M = $3.00 − $0.75 = $2.25/unit; Third-Party >20M = $3.00 − $0.25 = $2.75/unit
Set up equation (ignoring set-up cost for indifference-volume calculation): 2.50x = 2.25(20,000,000) + 2.75(x − 20,000,000)
New-plant breakeven on set-up cost: $52,500,000 ÷ $2.50 = 21,000,000 units (42% of annual volume; recovered in under one year at current production)
math.answer: The two options are equally attractive at 40 million units. Because CDC currently produces 50 million units per year (above 40 million), the new plant generates higher contribution. The set-up cost is recovered in under one year.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Suppose you are the governor of North Dakota. What factors might you consider in encouraging CDC to build the new plant and maintain its operations in your state?
questions.guidance: This creativity and structure question has no single right answer. Average candidates give a short, unstructured list. Good candidates generate several ideas but lack a clear structure. Great candidates organise their thinking into explicit categories (e.g. Personal/Political and State Government) and cover a comprehensive range of factors. The interviewer should probe until an exhaustive, justifiable list is produced.

brainstorming.prompt: As governor of North Dakota, what factors would you consider in encouraging CDC to build the new plant and maintain operations in your state?

categories.name: Personal / Political
ideas: Re-election prospects tied to job creation and economic growth
Risk of appearing to show corporate favoritism
Personal image — association with the pharmaceutical industry, environmental record of the new facility
Public perception of supporting local business vs. outsourcing jobs

categories.name: State Government
ideas: Employment: direct manufacturing jobs and indirect supply-chain jobs retained in North Dakota
Tax revenue: short-term incentives (tax breaks, grants) vs. long-term corporate and payroll tax base
National credibility and economic development signalling
Infrastructure investment spurred by plant construction
Community ties and social stability in the local area

recommendation: CDC should build the new plant in North Dakota

At CDC's current production volume of 50 million units per year, the new plant yields $2.50/unit contribution vs. the third-party blended contribution above 40 million units; the new plant is more profitable
The $52.5 million set-up cost is recouped in less than one year at current volume
risks: Volume risk: if annual production falls below 40 million units, the third-party option becomes more attractive
Capital risk: the $52.5 million upfront investment is at risk if demand declines significantly
Operational risk: building and running a new plant requires sustained manufacturing expertise and management bandwidth
next_steps: Validate demand projections to confirm volume will remain above 40 million units
Assess financing options for the $52.5 million capital outlay
Evaluate third-party contract terms in detail (duration, volume guarantees, quality standards) as a baseline comparison
Engage North Dakota state government regarding potential incentives for local construction
